article.overview: A subsurface radar sounder is a radar instrument that transmits radio pulses into the ground and records the echoes returned from buried boundaries, such as the contact between dust and bedrock or between successive lava flows. The round-trip time of each echo, combined with the wave speed in the material, gives the depth of the reflecting boundary [2]. The catalogue entry is a class of instrument rather than one design. This article therefore covers two geometries used on the Moon: orbital sounders that look down from a spacecraft, and surface radars carried on rovers that look into the regolith and rock beneath them [1][2]. Four examples are described: the Apollo 17 Lunar Sounder Experiment (ALSE), an orbital sounder flown in 1972 [4][5]; the Japanese SELENE (KAGUYA) Lunar Radar Sounder (LRS), an orbital sounder [1]; the Chang'e-4 Lunar Penetrating Radar (LPR) on the Yutu-2 rover, a surface radar [2]; and the Chang'e-3 LPR on the Yutu rover, a surface radar for which only summary results were accessed [3]. Each example uses different frequencies, antennas and depth performance, so their specifications must not be treated as directly comparable.
article.description: A radar sounder has four functional parts: a transmitter that generates the pulse, an antenna that radiates it and receives the echoes, a receiver that amplifies and digitises or records the returns, and a data chain that stores or downlinks the measurements. An orbital sounder places its antennas on a spacecraft far above the surface, so the strong surface return and weaker subsurface echoes must be separated in time and in power. A surface sounder places its antennas a few tens of centimetres above the ground, so the surface and subsurface returns are separated by a much shorter path [2]. The LRS on SELENE is described on the JAXA page as an HF radar operating at a nominal 5 MHz, with a 200 microsecond pulse width and a 10 kHz per microsecond frequency modulation (chirp), using two sets of 30 m tip-to-tip long dipole antennas [1]. The Chang'e-4 LPR has two channels: a low-frequency channel with a nominal central frequency of 60 MHz and a high-frequency channel with a nominal central frequency of 500 MHz [2]. ALSE operated a high-frequency pair (HF1 and HF2) and a VHF band, and its echoes were recorded photographically on film [5].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a lunar subsurface radar sounder is to map the layering, thickness and buried boundaries of the regolith and the volcanic rock beneath it. Those boundaries record the sequence of lava flows, impact deposits and regolith build-up that formed the surface [2][3][4]. ALSE was designed for substrate sounding, and its preliminary report states that the main goal of substrate sounding was likely to be achieved [4]. The JAXA page describes the LRS goal as mapping subsurface structure to depths of several kilometres [1]. The Chang'e-4 LPR was used to examine the shallow subsurface at its landing site on the lunar farside [2]. Applications include stratigraphy (ordering layers by depth and age), estimating the thickness of mare basalt and lava flows, identifying buried craters or faults, and characterising the top few metres of ground for surface operations. Some sounders have been proposed to search for water ice; none of the examples in this article is shown by the sources reviewed to have detected ice, so that application is not established here.
article.operating_principle: A radar pulse is an electromagnetic wave. As it travels through the regolith it loses energy (attenuation), and its speed depends on the material's electrical permittivity. Where the permittivity changes, for example between dust and a denser lava flow, part of the wave is reflected back. The sounder measures the delay between transmission and each echo. For a vertical path the depth is approximately d = v x t / 2, where v is the wave speed in the material and t is the round-trip time [2]. The Chang'e-4 study uses an average velocity of 0.16 m/ns for this conversion [2]. Lower frequencies are attenuated less and therefore penetrate deeper, but they resolve thinner layers less well. Higher frequencies resolve finer layers but penetrate less [2]. An orbital sounder also has to separate its active echoes from surface clutter and from natural radio and plasma emissions. The LRS therefore carries a passive receiver that listens to natural waves across 10 Hz to 30 MHz, in addition to the active sounder [1]. The LRS radar mode displays echo amplitude against range, as in the A-scope example shown in the physical specifications section [1].
article.scientific_importance: Images from orbit or from a rover camera show only the top surface. Subsurface radar is one of the few remote methods that can detect buried layer boundaries and measure their depth, which is needed to read the order of lava flows and deposits [2][3]. The Chang'e-3 LPR results summarised in the Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics abstract report regolith about 4 to 6 m thick and a deeper rock layer about 330 m deep, which the authors associate with a pause in mare basalt volcanism [3]. The Chang'e-4 study reports reflectors to roughly 40 m and states that penetration at the Chang'e-4 site was much greater than at the Chang'e-3 site, with a two-way travel time of about 500 ns at Chang'e-4 compared with about 150 ns at Chang'e-3 [2]. These results bear on the structure of the regolith, models of mare volcanism, and ground truth for orbital observations.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a subsurface radar sounder. Orbital and surface designs differ in frequency, antenna length, transmitted power and mass, and the values below belong to specific instruments. They are not directly comparable across designs. Where a value is a design target or a secondary-source figure, the example says so. Power values are electrical power consumption unless stated otherwise; radiated RF power is listed separately.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Sounder Experiment (ALSE)
examples.flight_status: Flown on Apollo 17 (1972) from the command and service module in lunar orbit
examples.frequencies: HF1 and HF2 (the high-frequency pair) and a VHF band. The Wikipedia specification table lists HF1 5.266 MHz, HF2 15.8 MHz and VHF 158 MHz; the same page's introduction rounds these to 5, 15 and 150 MHz. The two sets of values conflict and the primary report was not retrieved to resolve them.
examples.antennas: HF1 and HF2 share a centre-fed dipole whose two halves retract on opposite sides of the service module. The VHF channel uses a 7-element Yagi stowed near the main engine and deployed after launch. Antenna lengths are not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.penetration: Estimated depth of penetration: about 1300 m (HF1), 800 m (HF2) and 160 m (VHF). These are labelled as estimates, not measured values.
examples.recording: Received signal amplitude modulated a CRT swept at the pulse repetition rate, exposing 70 mm film. The VHF channel used an echo tracker to record the main surface return and the 70 microseconds of echo that follows. The film was retrieved by astronaut Ron Evans during an extravehicular activity on the return flight.
examples.dimensions: Not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.measured_results: Layers were reported at 0.9 km and 1.6 km below Mare Serenitatis and at 1.4 km below Mare Crisium. Combined with other observations, total basalt thickness was estimated at 2.4 to 3.4 km. The experiment did not detect the base of the mare basalts [5].
examples.qualification: Mass and power figures come from a secondary encyclopedia table and were not confirmed against the NASA preliminary science report, which was retrieved only as a record abstract [4][5].
examples.narrative: ALSE is the earliest example in this article. It used an HF dipole pair and a VHF antenna, and its data were recorded as film rather than in digital form. The HF pair is the sounding channel for deeper layers; the VHF channel records only the surface return and a short interval of echo. The secondary sources give the depths above as estimates, and this article does not treat them as measured values [5]. The reported layering beneath the mare basalts is an early demonstration of orbital subsurface sounding on the Moon [4][5]. The Aitken Basin profile shown below is a processed reproduction of ALSE data from the same mission [5][6].

examples.name: SELENE (KAGUYA) Lunar Radar Sounder (LRS)
examples.type: Lunar orbital radar sounder with passive plasma and radio receiver
examples.flight_status: Flown on the SELENE (KAGUYA) orbiter in lunar orbit; the figures below are JAXA specification values and were not checked against post-flight performance in this article
examples.frequencies: Sounder frequency 5 MHz (main frequency). Passive receiver (natural plasma and radio waves) 10 Hz to 30 MHz.
examples.antennas: Two sets of 30 m tip-to-tip long dipole antennas for the 5 MHz radar observation, per the JAXA page. Conference abstracts describe the elements as extended to about 15 m on each side of the spacecraft.
examples.penetration: Sounding depth 5 km (design value) and range resolution less than 100 m, per the JAXA page. The page's introduction says the instrument probes within a depth of several km.
examples.radar_waveform: Radiation power 800 W; pulse width 200 microseconds; modulation 10 kHz per microsecond.
examples.telemetry: High-speed telemetry 492 kbps; low-speed telemetry 176 kbps.
examples.recording: Digital telemetry to the spacecraft data system; the detailed chain is not described on the JAXA page.
examples.dimensions: Not stated on the JAXA page.
examples.operations: The JAXA page lists only pre-launch component tests at the Tsukuba Space Center radiowave test facility (20 to 22 December 2004 and 27 to 28 February 2006). Flight operation dates are not stated on that page. Conference abstracts found during research give antenna deployment in late October 2007 and operations until June 2009, but the dates differ between abstracts and were not verified against a primary report.
examples.measured_results: No measured flight results are quoted from a primary source in this article. The JAXA page provides design values only.
examples.qualification: The mass, power and telemetry values are from the JAXA specification table. The page does not separate design targets from measured flight values.
examples.narrative: LRS has the most complete primary specification set in this article, because it comes from the JAXA instrument page. The page describes the 5 MHz sounder as having a 5 km design sounding depth and a range resolution of less than 100 m. The schematic and the simulated A-scope show how the surface echo and the subsurface echo appear in the data. The A-scope is a simulation on the JAXA page and must not be read as measured lunar data [1]. The main unverified point is that the detailed post-flight paper (Ono and colleagues, Space Science Reviews, 2010) was located but not retrieved, so flight performance, the antenna deployment mechanism and the dimensions remain unverified in this article [1].

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Lunar Penetrating Radar (LPR) on the Yutu-2 rover
examples.type: Lunar surface penetrating radar on a rover (flown)
examples.flight_status: Flown on the Yutu-2 rover after the Chang'e-4 landing in the Von Karman crater area on the lunar farside (landed 3 January 2019 at 45.4446 degrees S, 177.5991 degrees E, as reported in the Science Advances paper)
examples.frequencies: Low-frequency channel: nominal central frequency 60 MHz, bandwidth 40 to 80 MHz. High-frequency channel: nominal central frequency 500 MHz, bandwidth 250 to 750 MHz. One source found during research gives a 450 MHz central frequency for the high-frequency bowtie antennas; the Science Advances paper states 500 MHz.
examples.antennas: Low-frequency channel: two monopoles, each 1.15 m long, spaced 0.8 m apart, mounted on the rear of the rover and suspended 0.6 m above the ground. High-frequency channel: one transmitting and two receiving bowtie antennas (CH2A and CH2B) on the underside of the rover, about 0.3 m above the ground.
examples.penetration: High-frequency channel reflectors were detected down to a two-way travel time of about 500 ns. Using the paper's average velocity of 0.16 m/ns, this corresponds to about 40 m, the deepest reflector reported. The Chang'e-3 comparison in the same paper is about 150 ns two-way. Vertical resolution is not stated in the paper; the paper gives a scatterer detection threshold of about half the wavelength (about 0.2 m).
examples.recording: Radargrams were recorded during the first two lunar days, over a route of about 106 m. Only the high-frequency channel B (CH2B) was analysed, because CH2A showed cross-talk. The low-frequency channel was not analysed because of coupling with the rover and the surface.
examples.dimensions: Antenna dimensions and mounting heights are given above; the total instrument mass and power are not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.measured_results: Layered reflectors at the Chang'e-4 site were detected to about 40 m, and the authors describe penetration as much greater than at the Chang'e-3 site.
examples.qualification: The frequency, antenna and route figures come from the Science Advances paper as accessed through the PMC record. The full paper figures and radargram images were not accessed directly.
examples.narrative: The Chang'e-4 LPR is the best-documented surface sounder in this article. Its two channels show the trade-off between depth and resolution: the 60 MHz channel was not analysed in the cited paper because of rover and surface coupling, and the 500 MHz channel penetrated to about 40 m [2]. The 500 ns two-way time and the 40 m depth are the study's values, with the 40 m figure converted using the paper's stated average velocity [2]. No radargram image from this payload could be verified as a direct, rights-cleared image asset, so none is included.

examples.name: Chang'e-3 Lunar Penetrating Radar (LPR) on the Yutu rover
examples.type: Lunar surface penetrating radar on a rover (flown)
examples.flight_status: Flown on the Yutu rover of the Chang'e-3 mission; detailed hardware specifications were not retrieved in this article
examples.frequencies: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed for this article.
examples.antennas: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.penetration: Preliminary results report regolith about 4 to 6 m thick and a rock layer about 330 m deep, from the RAA abstract. Press summaries give different deeper layer depths.
examples.recording: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
examples.measured_results: The 2014 RAA study reports regolith of about 4 to 6 m and a rock layer about 330 m deep. Press coverage in 2015 reported more than nine subsurface layers as a preliminary count.
examples.qualification: The RAA result is taken from the abstract found in search; the full text was not accessed. The 2015 layer count is from press coverage and is preliminary.
examples.narrative: The Chang'e-3 LPR is included because its results are the earlier surface-radar record for the Yutu rover and inform the comparison with Chang'e-4 [3]. Hardware values for this example have not been verified in this article, so it is described for its results only. The layer counts from press coverage have changed with later interpretation and must not be treated as settled [7].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Orbital designs carry antennas that are large compared with the spacecraft: the LRS uses 30 m tip-to-tip dipoles [1], and the ALSE HF antenna is a centre-fed dipole whose halves retract from the service module [5]. Surface designs use antennas that are small and fixed to the rover: the Chang'e-4 low-frequency monopoles are 1.15 m long and the high-frequency bowtie antennas sit about 0.3 m above the ground [2]. The antenna geometry is driven by the wavelength and the host platform, so the values are not directly comparable.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Recorded values: LRS mass 23.182 kg [1]; ALSE mass 43 kg from a secondary source [5]. Mass for the Chang'e-4 and Chang'e-3 radars is not publicly specified in the sources accessed. For spacecraft engineering, mass affects launch and landing budgets, and any future sounder would need a verified mass for its specific host.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Recorded values: LRS power 56.7 W [1]; ALSE power 103 W from a secondary source [5]. The LRS radiated RF power of 800 W [1] is an RF transmission level and is not the same quantity as electrical power consumption. Power for the Chang'e-4 and Chang'e-3 radars is not publicly specified in the sources accessed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar radar sounder works in vacuum, with extreme day-night temperature cycles, solar and galactic radiation, and fine dust. These conditions come from general lunar engineering and are not figures taken from the sources in this article. A surface radar must keep its antennas at a stable height and orientation over the lunar day and night, and it depends on the ground being sufficiently low-loss for deep sounding. The Chang'e-4 measurements were made during the first two lunar days [2]. An orbital sounder must deploy long antennas after launch and must separate its signals from spacecraft noise and from natural radio emissions. The LRS passive receiver covers 10 Hz to 30 MHz for that purpose [1]. LRS telemetry rates are 492 kbps (high speed) and 176 kbps (low speed) [1]. Attitude and pointing requirements for the orbital radars are not stated in the sources accessed.
article.limitations: Depth depends on the assumed wave speed in the material. The Chang'e-4 depth is an estimate from a stated average velocity [2]. Depth and resolution trade off against each other, so no single frequency resolves both deep and thin layers. Surface clutter and rover coupling can hide the response of a channel, as happened with the Chang'e-4 low-frequency channel [2]. Orbital estimates are labelled as estimates by their source [5]. Several specification values in this article come from secondary sources and have not been confirmed against primary instrument papers.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The examples in this article are of two kinds. Orbital sounders are integrated onto a spacecraft: ALSE on the Apollo command and service module and the LRS on the SELENE orbiter [1][5]. Surface radars are integrated onto a rover, as with the Chang'e-4 LPR on Yutu-2 [2]. The transportation chain is therefore different for each. The sources accessed do not give interface data for a future subsurface radar sounder on a named lander or spacecraft, so no compatibility is asserted here.
transportation_process: Orbital sounder: integrate the instrument electronics and stowed antennas into the spacecraft on Earth.

Orbital sounder: launch on a launch vehicle and transfer to the Moon; deploy the long antennas after launch or in orbit, as the design requires. ALSE deployed its VHF antenna after launch; the LRS deployment mechanism is not described on the JAXA page.
Orbital sounder: enter lunar orbit, commission the active and passive modes, then operate during science orbits and downlink the data.
Surface radar: integrate the radar antennas on the rover, with the low-frequency monopoles on the rear and the high-frequency bowtie antennas on the underside at fixed heights [2].
Surface radar: deliver the rover to the surface, deploy it, and operate the radar during the lunar day, with surface and rover coupling characterised before data are analysed [2].
All cases: confirm mass, power, thermal, mechanical and data interfaces against the host's interface control document. These interfaces are not verified for any named host in this article.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: ALSE: the HF dipole halves retracted on opposite sides of the service module, and the VHF Yagi was deployed after launch [5]. LRS: two sets of long dipole antennas were extended from the spacecraft after launch; the JAXA page does not describe the mechanism [1]. Chang'e-4 LPR: the antennas are fixed to the rover at stated heights, and no deployment mechanism is described in the cited paper [2].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: ALSE on Apollo 17 is the historical example for an orbital sounder. Its film record was retrieved by an astronaut during an extravehicular activity on the return flight, according to a secondary source [5]. The Chang'e-4 rover collected radar data during its first two lunar days along a route of about 106 m [2]. The LRS on SELENE is documented through its instrument page and conference abstracts [1].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. A future sounder would need its mass, power, thermal, mechanical and data requirements checked against the host's interface documents. The ALSE and LRS examples flew on lunar orbiters and the Chang'e-4 radar flew on a rover, so each demonstrates only its own host arrangement [1][2][5].

article.historical_significance: ALSE was flown on Apollo 17 and provided an early orbital record of subsurface layering beneath the mare basalts, with preliminary depths reported in the Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report [4][5]. The LRS on SELENE extended orbital sounding with a 5 MHz instrument and a design depth of 5 km [1]. The Chang'e-3 and Chang'e-4 LPRs demonstrated surface radar sounding of the shallow subsurface, with the Chang'e-4 radar reaching about 40 m at the farside site [2][3]. Together these examples show two complementary approaches: orbital sounding of deeper structure and surface radar of the upper layers. The Aitken Basin profile shown below is a processed reproduction of ALSE data [5][6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- ALSE frequencies: the Wikipedia specification table gives 5.266, 15.8 and 158 MHz, while the same page's introduction gives 5, 15 and 150 MHz. The NTRS record abstract does not state the frequencies, so the conflict is unresolved [4][5].
- ALSE mass (43 kg), power (103 W) and penetration estimates come from a secondary encyclopedia table and were not confirmed against a primary report [5].
- LRS: the specifications are from the JAXA instrument page and are not separated into design targets and measured flight values. The 2010 Space Science Reviews paper was located but not retrieved, so the LRS dimensions, post-flight performance and deployment mechanism remain unverified [1].
- LRS operation dates: the JAXA page gives only pre-launch test dates. Conference abstract dates for antenna deployment and end of operations conflict and are unverified.
- Chang'e-4 LPR: the 500 MHz nominal central frequency conflicts with a 450 MHz figure found in a second source. Vertical resolution is not stated. The 40 m depth is derived from the stated two-way time and average velocity [2].
- Chang'e-3 LPR: hardware specifications were not retrieved, and the RAA results were taken from the abstract only [3]. The preliminary count of more than nine layers is press-reported and has been revised by later work [7].
- No payload in this article is shown to have detected water ice, and no lunar landing site or location recommendation is made, as deferred by the user.
- Image rights: the two JAXA images were verified as direct assets on the official page; the ALSE image is from Wikimedia Commons and its original NASA source document was not located [6].

data_quality_notes: ALSE frequencies conflict between sources: Wikipedia specification table 5.266, 15.8 and 158 MHz versus its introduction 5, 15 and 150 MHz; the primary NTRS record abstract does not state the frequencies. Unresolved.
ALSE mass (43 kg), power (103 W) and penetration estimates (1300, 800, 160 m) come from a secondary encyclopedia table, not a primary report. The source labels the penetration values as estimates.

ALSE layer depths (0.9 and 1.6 km in Serenitatis; 1.4 km in Crisium; 2.4-3.4 km total basalt estimate) come from a secondary source citing the Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report; the primary text was not retrieved.

LRS specifications come from the JAXA instrument page and are design values; post-flight performance is not separated. Ono et al. (2010, Space Science Reviews) was located but not retrieved; dimensions, deployment mechanism and flight performance are unverified.
LRS operating dates are not on the JAXA page. Conference abstract dates for antenna deployment (29 vs 30 October 2007) and end of operations (June 2009) conflict and are unverified.
LRS antenna description: the JAXA page gives 30 m tip-to-tip; a conference abstract describes elements extended to about 15 m on each side. These are consistent but phrased differently.

Chang'e-4 LPR: the 500 MHz nominal central frequency (Science Advances) conflicts with a 450 MHz figure in a second source. Vertical resolution is not stated; the about 0.2 m value is a scatterer detection threshold, not a resolution specification.
The Chang'e-4 40 m depth is derived from the 500 ns two-way time and the paper's stated average velocity of 0.16 m/ns; it is not a directly measured depth.
Chang'e-4 radargram figures were not accessed: publisher pages required login and PMC was accessed only as a record summary. No verified direct radargram image asset was found, so none is included.

Chang'e-3 LPR hardware specifications (frequencies, antennas, mass, power) were not retrieved. RAA 2014 results (regolith about 4-6 m; rock layer about 330 m) come from the abstract as found in search; the full text was not accessed.
The press-reported count of more than nine subsurface layers for Chang'e-3 (2015) is preliminary and secondary; later interpretation has revised the layer picture.

The ALSE image is from Wikimedia Commons; its licence statement attributes it to NASA, but the original NASA source document was not located, so reuse rights are not independently confirmed. It is not an official NASA asset page.
Environmental requirements for a lunar sounder (vacuum, thermal cycling, radiation, dust) are general engineering context, not figures from the cited sources.
No evidence was found that any example detected water ice; ice detection is not claimed.
No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted; interface verification was not performed for any named host.
Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
